motion: Do morality and meaning point to God?

bridges.description: Connect objective moral norms and a higher human calling to a transcendent divine ground.
Argue that morality extending across persons, cultures, and eras requires a source that likewise transcends them.
Use recurring values and Golden Rule expectations across cultures as support for objective moral values and duties.
Distinguish ordinary self-chosen purposes from a higher calling for which humans were put here.
Present Jesus, divine accountability, mercy, and justice as content for the theistic moral and purposive framework.
Show that objective moral facts and meaningful lives can be understood without a divine ground.
Ground objective moral facts in facts about conscious experience, well-being, and unnecessary suffering.
Separate objective moral facts and conditional reasons from external categorical obligations.
Explain shared moral intuitions through social and evolutionary pressures without inferring metaphysical moral duties.
Argue that finite, self-shaped meaning is not undermined by lacking an externally assigned eternal purpose.
Test whether biblical portrayals, salvation, and endless afterlife cohere with moral perfection and personal identity.

sections.title: Objective moral facts and well-being
sections.rationale: Establishes the shared and disputed meanings of moral objectivity before either side argues about its source.

sections.title: Transcendent grounding and categorical duties
sections.rationale: Addresses whether moral facts require a transcendent source and whether facts themselves entail duties.

sections.title: Moral motivation and divine command
sections.rationale: Tests whether divine obligation adds motivational force and whether commands can be separated from consequences for conscious beings.

sections.title: Cross-cultural agreement and naturalistic explanation
sections.rationale: Tests what cultural commonalities can establish and whether evolutionary explanation changes their metaphysical significance.

sections.title: Higher purpose and finite meaning
sections.rationale: Directly compares a God-given calling with finite, self-shaped purpose and meaning.

sections.title: Christianity, salvation, and eternal life
sections.rationale: Examines whether the proposed Christian framework supplies coherent moral purpose and an attractive eternal end.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: Moral discussion can be objective in the same sense that medicine can be objective.
moves.warrant: Some claims about harm, including that rat poison kills and rape is wrong, can be true independently of a person's opinion.
moves.inference: A secular speaker can affirm objective moral claims without accepting moral relativism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Clifton rejecting the relativist label and ends at the close of his medicine-and-harm analogy, before Thomason's reply.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton explicitly rejects the relativist label and gives a sustained analogy before Thomason answers.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Clifton's foundational account of moral objectivity.

burdenContact.rationale: Defines the secular ground for objective moral facts.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: People share objective moral values centered on life and fair treatment.
moves.warrant: People commonly rally against taking life or treating others unfairly and regard valuing life as self-evident.
moves.inference: Shared moral recognition supports the reality of objective values.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Captures Thomason's complete first statement of shared life and fairness values without Clifton's following qualification.
moves.attributionRationale: The turn follows Clifton's answer and is framed in Thomason's first-person agreement.
moves.importanceRationale: It states Thomason's initial moral-value premise.

burdenContact.rationale: Supplies the claimed common values later used in the grounding argument.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: Objective moral facts do not automatically entail intrinsic value or objective duties.
moves.warrant: Moral facts can concern conscious experience and well-being while obligations remain conditional on desired states of the world.
moves.inference: Agreement that some moral claims are objective does not settle the stronger theistic claim about values and duties.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Starts at Clifton's explicit request to parse Thomason's terminology after her intervening turn and ends after his complete distinction between facts and obligations.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I think ultimately morality reduces to well-being
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton explicitly asks to parse Thomason's terminology and sustains the facts, well-being, and obligation distinction until she replies.
moves.importanceRationale: This qualification controls Clifton's actual burden throughout the exchange.

burdenContact.rationale: Establishes the fact-duty distinction central to his route.

responseComponents.description: Qualifies the move from shared objective moral claims to intrinsic values and duties.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: Reported survey and cross-disciplinary research identify recurring moral foundations such as care and fairness.
moves.warrant: Thomason cites Jonathan Haidt's survey and literature review as identifying foundations shared across people, with political groups weighting them differently.
moves.inference: Recurring foundations supply empirical support for cross-human moral commonalities, though the report does not by itself establish their metaphysical source.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Thomason introducing the reported survey and literature review and ends after her complete description of the five foundations and differing political weighting.
moves.attributionRationale: Thomason narrates the reported study continuously after Clifton says he does not know its argument.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a distinct empirical premise for her cross-cultural commonality line.

burdenContact.rationale: Offers reported empirical support for recurring moral foundations.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: Objective morality that transcends generations, peoples, and eras should have a transcendent source.
moves.warrant: A source located only in changing human opinions or consequences would not match morality's claimed cross-era reach.
moves.inference: A transcendent ground is a better candidate for the source of objective morality.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Isolates Thomason's complete source argument from her preceding description of consequentialism and Clifton's reply.
moves.attributionRationale: Thomason announces 'I would actually make the argument' and completes it before Clifton responds.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Thomason's clearest direct bridge from moral objectivity to transcendence.

burdenContact.rationale: States the principal inference from objective morality to a transcendent source.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: Theistic and well-being accounts can both make objective claims while defining moral wrongness by different standards.
moves.warrant: A theist may identify wrongness with conflict with God's nature, while a secular account identifies it with unnecessary suffering.
moves.inference: Objectivity alone does not select the divine standard over the well-being standard.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Clifton accepting the need to discuss the source and ends after his full comparison of the two standards.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton directly contrasts 'when you say' with 'I'm saying' in a sustained reply.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly challenges the inference from objectivity to a divine source.

burdenContact.rationale: Shows how the well-being standard can remain objective without God.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the claim that moral objectivity uniquely favors transcendence.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: Acts such as rape are objectively wrong because they violate life, liberty, and justice.
moves.warrant: The act violates the victim's life and liberty and is unjust in every contemplated instance.
moves.inference: Concrete moral judgments are anchored in objective values rather than preference.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Captures Thomason's full application of the value-duty terminology to an unambiguous example.
moves.attributionRationale: The first-person explanation follows Thomason's reference to William Lane Craig and remains continuous.
moves.importanceRationale: It makes her abstract values account concrete.

burdenContact.rationale: Connects claimed objective values to judgments of right and wrong.

responseComponents.description: Reasserts a values-based account of objective wrongness.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: A fact about an act's moral status does not itself state what anyone ought to do.
moves.warrant: The proposition that rape is wrong and the proposition that one is obligated not to rape are conceptually distinct.
moves.inference: Combining moral facts with duties requires an additional argument.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Starts with Clifton's correction of the duty definition and ends at his explicit conclusion that he distinguishes the two ideas.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton explicitly addresses Thomason and Craig in one uninterrupted clarification.
moves.importanceRationale: It isolates the exact inferential step disputed by Clifton.

burdenContact.rationale: Denies that objective status by itself creates categorical obligation.

responseComponents.description: Separates the act's objective wrongness from an obligation governing action.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: The Golden Rule is a cross-cultural moral duty.
moves.warrant: Forms of the Golden Rule appear across cultures, religions, and humanist commitments.
moves.inference: Its recurrence supports a universal prescriptive moral norm.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins after Clifton's distinction and ends with Thomason's complete cross-cultural Golden Rule claim.
moves.attributionRationale: Thomason introduces the is-ought distinction and supplies the cross-cultural example.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the first direct cross-cultural support for the pro route.

burdenContact.rationale: Uses alleged universality to support a duty rather than a local preference.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: The Golden Rule can be a wise social principle without God or objective categorical morality.
moves.warrant: Evolved social beings benefit from fairness and cooperation, and societies are happier when members follow the rule.
moves.inference: Cross-cultural usefulness can explain endorsement descriptively without establishing a divine prescription.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Captures Clifton's whole reply from the rule's pre-Christian history through his conclusion that the claim is descriptive.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton speaks continuously after Thomason's Golden Rule claim.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies a secular explanation of the same cross-cultural observation.

burdenContact.rationale: Explains shared norms through cooperative social life.

responseComponents.description: Recasts universality and usefulness as descriptive rather than divine prescription.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: The principal difference between the speakers is that shared objective values are grounded in a transcendent Lord rather than consequences.
moves.warrant: Both speakers recognize cross-human values, while Thomason assigns their source beyond humanity.
moves.inference: Shared moral facts become evidence for divine grounding when their source is identified as transcendent.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Captures Thomason's concise comparison of agreed values and disputed source before Clifton corrects the desire formulation.
moves.attributionRationale: Thomason explicitly compares 'you and I' and states her own source claim.
moves.importanceRationale: It restates the motion-level source dispute in the second exchange.

burdenContact.rationale: Directly links objective morality to God.

responseComponents.description: Contrasts the well-being account with a transcendent divine source.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: Moral oughts can be conditional on aims without an external cosmic obligation.
moves.warrant: If one wants to be moral, helping another can follow as a reason, while no separate divine force is needed to bind the act.
moves.inference: Practical moral reasons remain available even if categorical divine obligations are rejected.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Starts with Clifton correcting the claim that his standard is desire and ends with his question about whether source is the only difference.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton sustains the first-person example and closes by questioning Thomason.
moves.importanceRationale: It gives the positive conditional account replacing divine categorical duties.

burdenContact.rationale: Explains how reasons guide conduct without external categorical binding.

responseComponents.description: Corrects the characterization of well-being as mere desire and denies a need for divine binding.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: Nothing is intrinsically valuable or intrinsically right or wrong; reasons make things right or wrong.
moves.warrant: Moral status depends on reasons rather than being an intrinsic property of an act or life.
moves.inference: A reasons-based account can differ from Thomason's intrinsic-value language even when both recognize objective facts.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Clifton identifying another difference between the views and ends with his completed reasons thesis immediately before Thomason answers.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton states the first-person thesis continuously; Thomason's response beginning at E0666 is excluded.
moves.importanceRationale: It sharpens the nonintrinsic basis of Clifton's account.

burdenContact.rationale: Locates moral status in assessable reasons rather than intrinsic properties.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: Divine sanctions do not solve the motivational problem posed by someone who rejects the relevant values.
moves.warrant: A would-be wrongdoer who does not care about hell or even wants it cannot be moved by that sanction any more than by secular moral appeal.
moves.inference: Adding categorical divine obligation provides no practical leverage absent shared motivations.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Clifton identifying the alleged liability of prescriptive theism and ends after his explicit conclusion that the added obligation supplies no utility beyond existing moral facts.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton develops the killer and hell example in a sustained turn, explicitly contrasting Thomason's view with his.
moves.importanceRationale: This is a developed symmetry challenge to the claimed motivational advantage of divine duties.

burdenContact.rationale: Argues that categorical divine obligation adds no motivational force without shared values.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the practical advantage of grounding duties in a transcendent Lord.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: A stipulated divine command that made required acts produce universal misery and forbidden acts produce universal flourishing would pressure moral intuition toward well-being rather than bare obligation.
moves.warrant: The thought experiment reverses every consequence while stipulating that God still labels the misery-producing acts obligatory.
moves.inference: Moral judgment appears to depend on consequences for conscious beings rather than obligation alone.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Clifton introducing the thought experiment and ends in E0833 after the complete question 'what I ought to do'; the event's trailing 'yeah you'd probably' is mixed handoff context only and is not credited as Thomason's answer or concession.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton clearly owns the developed hypothetical and the complete question through 'what I ought to do'; the unavoidable trailing words in E0833 begin an unresolved mixed handoff and carry no argumentative credit.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Audio verification is required to resolve the E0833 handoff after Clifton's completed question before adjudication.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a distinct test of whether divine obligation can be divorced from well-being.

burdenContact.rationale: Tests bare obligation against consequences for universal suffering and flourishing.

responseComponents.description: Tests whether a divine source remains morally decisive when stipulated commands oppose all well-being.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: Cross-cultural studies identifying common is-ought judgments are proposed as a method for supporting universal moral duties.
moves.warrant: If independent cultural findings converge on the same oughts, Thomason asks whether that convergence warrants calling them objective.
moves.inference: Empirical commonality is offered as a bridge from observed judgments to objective duties.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Thomason explicitly asking how universal moral duties could be shown and ends with her completed proposed inference from cross-cultural commonality to objectivity.
moves.attributionRationale: Thomason owns the sustained methodological question; Clifton's request for clarification begins afterward.
moves.importanceRationale: It states the exact empirical-to-normative bridge later contested by Clifton.

burdenContact.rationale: Connects cross-cultural commonality to the claimed objectivity of duties.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: Cross-cultural research reports a common judgment that societies ought to be more humane.
moves.warrant: Thomason describes a study in which the desired level of humane orientation exceeded reported practice across countries.
moves.inference: A repeated is-ought pattern supplies evidence relevant to universal moral duties.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Thomason naming the study and ends once she completes the cross-country humane-orientation observation and theological suggestion.
moves.attributionRationale: Thomason narrates the study in a continuous turn; caption recognition is preserved exactly.
moves.importanceRationale: It is her main empirical example for cross-cultural oughts.

burdenContact.rationale: Offers cross-cultural agreement as evidence for universal norms.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: Cross-cultural moral patterns do not by themselves demonstrate objective morality or its metaphysical source.
moves.warrant: Evolution and social selection can explain why human brains project similar moral intuitions even if no corresponding metaphysical property exists.
moves.inference: Observed agreement is compatible with a naturalistic genealogy and cannot carry the proposed metaphysical conclusion alone.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Clifton's direct response to the study and ends at his explicit conclusion that psychology does not establish metaphysics.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton's reply is uninterrupted and explicitly distinguishes psychology from metaphysics.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly challenges the evidential bridge from commonality to divine or objective grounding.

burdenContact.rationale: Supplies the alternative evolutionary and social explanation.

responseComponents.description: Denies that the reported cross-cultural pattern establishes metaphysical moral facts.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: Atheists can have everyday purposes, but they lack a higher God-given calling on Thomason's view.
moves.warrant: Work, family, and daily aims supply ordinary purpose, while the higher level is specifically divine.
moves.inference: The motion concerns a qualified higher purpose rather than denying all purpose to atheists.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Starts with Clifton raising Thomason's purpose claim and includes Thomason's explicit correction through her completed everyday-versus-higher-purpose distinction, ending before Clifton's reply.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton frames the topic in E1649–E1657; Thomason's owned answer is the explicit correction and distinction in E1650 and E1658–E1664. The claim credits only that answer, not Clifton's framing.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves the qualified pro burden on the meaning half of the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: Distinguishes higher divine calling from ordinary purposes.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: Lacking an externally assigned teleological purpose creates no internal problem for an atheist worldview.
moves.warrant: Clifton openly accepts that there is no creator-assigned purpose and does not regard that absence as a defect.
moves.inference: The absence of divine purpose does not entail that a life cannot be meaningful on its own terms.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Isolates Clifton's direct response accepting the lack of creator-type purpose and challenging its alleged cost.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton speaks in the first person and directly asks whether accepting the point creates an internal problem.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly rejects the claimed negative implication for atheism.

burdenContact.rationale: Accepts the absence of divine assignment while denying that it defeats meaning.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the distinction while denying that the missing higher tier is a worldview defect.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: Human meaning-seeking and individual gifts fit the view that people are put here for a reason and should discover their calling.
moves.warrant: Humans naturally seek meaning and purpose, and each person has gifts that can be developed toward what they are supposed to do.
moves.inference: These features of human life point toward an assigned higher purpose rather than only constructed satisfaction.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins when Thomason answers Clifton's internal-problem question and ends with her complete gifts-and-calling account before he turns to her tweet.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we're all put here for a reason
moves.attributionRationale: Thomason's first-person view begins after Clifton finishes his challenge and continues uninterrupted through her 'bottom line idea.'
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies her positive warrant for higher calling beyond the initial distinction.

burdenContact.rationale: Connects human meaning-seeking and gifts to an assigned divine calling.

responseComponents.description: Answers that the absence of divine purpose overlooks natural meaning-seeking and individual gifts understood as a calling.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: If atheism is taken to its conclusion, life lacks ultimate meaning because humans are cosmically accidental and soon forgotten.
moves.warrant: Without a divine framework, human lives occupy a small, random place and leave little enduring remembrance.
moves.inference: The desire for nontransient meaning can rationally point people toward theism or deism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Thomason's own advocacy after Clifton finishes quoting and questioning her tweet, and ends after her complete inference toward theism or deism.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton's quoted setup at E1697–E1710 is excluded; Thomason's owned argument begins with 'to me yeah I think' at E1711.
moves.importanceRationale: This is her strongest explicit argument from atheism to loss of ultimate meaning.

burdenContact.rationale: Directly claims that God is needed for ultimate meaning.

responseComponents.description: Argues that accepting no divine purpose carries a nihilistic consequence.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: A life does not lose value because it ends or is eventually forgotten.
moves.warrant: Demanding remembrance reflects ego, and a movie can be valuable partly because it has a finite narrative and resolution.
moves.inference: Finitude is compatible with meaningful experience and does not force nihilism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Captures Clifton's complete ego objection and finite-movie analogy through its contrast with endless continuation.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton explicitly answers the forgetting claim with a sustained analogy.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the principal secular reply to the nihilism argument.

burdenContact.rationale: Explains how finite experiences retain value and narrative meaning.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the inference from ending or being forgotten to meaninglessness.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: If externally assigned purpose is required for meaningful existence, God's own uncreated existence appears purposeless.
moves.warrant: God has no creator or prior cause assigning a purpose, yet Thomason does not infer that God is a nihilist.
moves.inference: The standard that makes created life meaningful cannot simply be external assignment without creating an asymmetry.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins at Clifton's explicit question and ends after his conclusion that God's purposelessness does not seem to trouble Thomason.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton addresses Thomason directly and maintains the hypothetical argument throughout.
moves.importanceRationale: It tests the consistency of the external-purpose requirement.

burdenContact.rationale: Challenges external assignment as a necessary condition of meaningful existence.

responseComponents.description: Applies the external-purpose condition to God to test its consistency.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: God's mode of being differs from created doing, while belief in God gives humans external accountability.
moves.warrant: God is described as always existing and unchanging rather than as a created agent needing an assigned purpose.
moves.inference: The lack of a creator for God does not erase the purpose God supplies to humans.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Captures Thomason's immediate being-doing answer and its concrete accountability implication.
moves.attributionRationale: Thomason begins with 'being doing distinction' and answers Clifton's God-purpose challenge.
moves.importanceRationale: It is her direct reply to the regress-style objection.

burdenContact.rationale: Uses divine being and accountability to answer the purpose challenge.

responseComponents.description: Answers that God is uncreated being and supplies accountability to created persons.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: Given the preceding stipulation that the appearance eventually convinced him Christianity is true, Clifton would remain open while asking moral questions.
moves.warrant: He accepts a morally perfect being in principle but regards some biblical portrayals as morally mistaken and possibly shaped by fallible human authors.
moves.inference: Conceding divine existence under the stipulated hypothetical would not by itself establish every scriptural portrayal as morally authoritative.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Clifton's owned answer after Thomason's question and repeated conviction stipulation, and ends after his complete fallible-authorship explanation.
moves.attributionRationale: Thomason owns the preceding hypothetical and stipulation; Clifton's selected first-person response begins at E1827 and remains continuous.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves the source note's key qualification and separates generic theism from scriptural authority.

burdenContact.rationale: Tests whether the specific Christian portrayal follows morally from conceded divine existence.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: A salvation system requiring acknowledgment of rescue from default damnation appears inconsistent with moral perfection.
moves.warrant: On Clifton's description, rescue is withheld unless the person credits and believes in the rescuer, leaving nonbelievers subject to eternal torment.
moves.inference: The specific salvation structure requires moral reconciliation even if a perfect being is possible in principle.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Clifton's separate salvation objection and ends with his stated need to ask questions and reconcile it.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton speaks continuously in the first person and marks this as an additional issue.
moves.importanceRationale: It is his direct moral challenge to the offered Christian framework.

burdenContact.rationale: Challenges the consistency of salvation with moral perfection.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: Jesus manifests love and reconciles divine mercy with justice by taking punishment for human sin.
moves.warrant: Following Jesus is framed as aligning with love; atonement permits forgiveness while satisfying justice.
moves.inference: Christianity provides a moral model and a route to reconciliation rather than the morally defective system Clifton describes.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Starts with Thomason turning to Jesus as the moral example and ends after her complete mercy, justice, and atonement explanation.
moves.attributionRationale: Thomason's first-person biblical explanation directly follows Clifton's moral objections.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the main positive Christian answer within the retained final exchange.

burdenContact.rationale: Supplies the Christian content of love, mercy, justice, and reconciliation.

responseComponents.description: Presents atonement as a reconciliation of mercy and justice.

moves.speaker: SJ Thomason
moves.claim: Objections to heaven can rest on a mistaken picture of it as an unpleasant continuation of earthly life.
moves.warrant: Thomason suggests that some atheists or agnostics imagine heaven as something like earth forever and reject that imagined condition.
moves.inference: A more accurate account of heaven may answer the objection that eternal life is undesirable.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Thomason introducing the additional heaven issue and ends after her complete description of the mistaken earth-forever picture, before Clifton replies.
moves.attributionRationale: Thomason introduces this as 'the other thing' and completes the contrast before Clifton's 'no no' response.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the immediate pro target of Clifton's later eternity objection.

burdenContact.rationale: Defends the promised Christian end by distinguishing heaven from endless ordinary earthly life.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: The stated principle of Jesus as love does not by itself answer the concern that the concrete salvation arrangement resembles extortion.
moves.warrant: A loving parent who treated a child as Clifton says God treats humanity would be condemned rather than praised.
moves.inference: The abstract love principle requires reconciliation with the specific conditions attached to salvation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Clifton acknowledging Thomason's Jesus principle and ends after his complete parent analogy and express return to the principle.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton directly refers back to 'everything that you said about Jesus' and sustains the objection until returning to the principle.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the immediate reply to Thomason's love-and-atonement account.

burdenContact.rationale: Tests whether the abstract love principle fits the concrete salvation arrangement.

responseComponents.description: Acknowledges the love principle but argues that the concrete salvation relationship still appears coercive.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.claim: An endless conscious experience would become torment, while changing a person enough to enjoy it threatens personal identity and raises a free-will problem.
moves.warrant: Any fixed positive mental state extended forever would become unbearable; if God alters psychology to prevent that, the resulting subject may no longer be the same person.
moves.inference: Eternal heaven does not straightforwardly supply desirable ultimate meaning.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins when Clifton turns specifically to heaven and ends at his complete conclusion about never-ending conscious experience before excluded audience material begins.
moves.attributionRationale: Clifton's sustained first-person argument follows Thomason's account and remains within the retained interval.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly tests the desirability and coherence of the eternal-purpose endpoint.

burdenContact.rationale: Challenges eternal life as a coherent benefit and preserves the identity/free-will qualification.

responseComponents.description: Answers that the problem is endless conscious experience itself, not merely an image of ordinary earthly life continuing.

retainedMajorLines.description: Objective well-being facts, shared values, and the fact-duty distinction.
Transcendent source, competing standards, and categorical versus conditional obligation.
Golden Rule, cross-cultural humane orientation, and naturalistic explanation.
Higher calling, finite meaning, forgetting, and the God-purpose challenge.
Stipulated conviction, biblical portrayal, salvation, Jesus, and endless afterlife.

omissions.reason: Topic setup and named-debate references; the first substantive positions are retained immediately afterward.
Brief disagreement over whether the Golden Rule claim is prescriptive ends at an excluded conversational transition and adds no developed warrant.
Biographical account of Clifton's earlier relativism and later definitional clarity repeats the selected objective-facts position.
Additional cultural and terminology examples repeat the selected naturalistic and reasons-based lines.
Further qualification and evolutionary elaboration are represented by the selected complete reply ending at E0962.
General setup about morality as rational enterprise is represented by the selected, more developed motivation and divine-command challenges that follow.
The remaining brief mixed assents have unresolved ownership and are not used as a Thomason concession; Clifton's recap repeats the selected thought experiment's stated purpose.
Clifton quotes Thomason's tweet and poses a question; the inventory credits Thomason only from the start of her own subsequent advocacy.
Thomason poses and repeats the Jesus-appearance hypothetical while Clifton clarifies its terms; the selected Clifton move begins only with his owned answer after eventual conviction is stipulated.
Named-book and author setup leading to the separately retained moral-foundations report; it adds no independent inference beyond locating the discussion.

Thomason characterizes Sam Harris as grounding well-being in shared desire, and Clifton corrects that well-being facts are independent of desire. Clifton's substantive correction is already represented in the selected E0234–E0290 move, which states that objective facts about subjects and well-being are distinct from obligations; the named-author exchange adds no separate motion-level burden.

Clifton asks whether Thomason means categorical duties and distinguishes them from moral facts; that distinction is already retained in E0432–E0455, while the remaining lines pivot toward audience context.
